messages.subject: Using "group.label" changes results of CFA
messages.subject_clean: Using "group.label" changes results of CFA
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I noticed that swapping the orders of groups when testing weak measurement invariance in a dataset where the factor loadings are not equal across groups changes the estimated factor loadings. Specifically, the estimates are "pulled" towards the data generating values of the group that serves as the reference group. I assumed the results would be equal, no matter which group is analyzed first (shows up in the dataset first).
Is this behaviour intended? Or am I doing something wrong/misunderstanding something? It worries me a bit because right now the results of my analysis change depending on the order of the observations in the dataset (which group shows up first).

Here is the code I used:
library(MASS)
library(lavaan)

set.seed(123)
nobs = 10000

#### generate factor scores ####
phi <- matrix(c(1, .5, .5, 1), ncol = 2) # factor (co)variances, identical across groups
alpha <- c(0, 0) # factor means, identical across groups

eta1 <- mvrnorm(nobs, mu = alpha, Sigma = phi, empirical=T) # generate factor scores group 1
eta2 <- mvrnorm(nobs, mu = alpha, Sigma = phi, empirical=T) # generate factor scores group 2

#### prepare matrices (standardized loadings) ####
## group 1
loadings1_fac1 <- c(.6, .5, .8, .9, .9)
loadings1_fac2 <- c(.5, .7, .9, .8, .8)
lambda1 <- matrix(c(loadings1_fac1, rep(0, 5), rep(0, 5), loadings1_fac2), nrow = 10, ncol = 2) # prepare loadings matrix
errorvar1 <- as.vector(c(1 - loadings1_fac1^2, 1 - loadings1_fac2^2)) # compute error variances
theta1 <- matrix(0, nrow = 10, ncol = 10) # create error covariance matrix
diag(theta1) <- errorvar1 # impute error variances on theta diagonal (assuming uncorrelated errors)

## group 2
loadings2_fac1 <- c(.6, .5, .8, .4, .4)
loadings2_fac2 <- c(.5, .7, .9, .3, .3)
lambda2 <- matrix(c(loadings2_fac1, rep(0, 5), rep(0, 5), loadings2_fac2), nrow = 10, ncol = 2) # prepare loadings matrix
errorvar2 <- as.vector(c(1 - loadings2_fac1^2, 1 - loadings2_fac2^2)) # compute error variances
theta2 <- matrix(0, nrow = 10, ncol = 10) # create error covariance matrix
diag(theta2) <- errorvar2 # impute error variances on theta diagonal (assuming uncorrelated errors)

#### generate errors and then observed scores (without intercepts) ####
epsilon1 <- mvrnorm(nrow(eta1), mu = rep(0, 10), Sigma = theta1, empirical=T) # errors in group 1
epsilon2 <- mvrnorm(nrow(eta2), mu = rep(0, 10), Sigma = theta2, empirical=T) # errors in group 2

df.1 <- as.data.frame(eta1 %*% t(lambda1) + epsilon1) # generate indicator scores in group 1
df.2 <- as.data.frame(eta2 %*% t(lambda2) + epsilon2) # generate indicator scores in group 2
df.1$group <- 1 # add grouping variable
df.2$group <- 2 # add grouping variable
df <- rbind(df.1, df.2) # combine the two dataframes

#### analyze the data ####
model <- "
    f1 =~ V1 + V2 + V3 + V4 + V5
    f2 =~ V6 + V7 + V8 + V9 + V10
    "

fit1 <- cfa(model, data = df, std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE, orthogonal = TRUE,
            group = "group", group.equal = c("loadings"))

fit2 <- cfa(model, data = df, std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE, orthogonal = TRUE,
           group = "group", group.equal = c("loadings"), group.label = c("2", "1"))

lavInspect(fit1, what = "est")$'1'$lambda
lavInspect(fit2, what = "est")$'1'$lambda
# the estimated factor loadings are not equal across the two fit objects

If no and if you are interested in the relative importance of (correlated) IV on a DV (multiple regression) you could apply the Shapley decomposition:  https://wernerantweiler.ca/blog.php?item=2014-10-10 This is easily implementable with latent IV/DV.

> Subject: Compare IV-DV regression parameter between two seperate models.

> Hi Everyone,
>       Here we wanted to check the strongest method of comparing a single parameter between SEM models. In this case we have the same DV but different IV's and thus measurement models. E.g., a range of mental health causes. Each of these models have the same DV, Depression. We want to compare the strength of the regression parameter between each of these models - that is, which IV has the strongest relationship with depression.
>
> The solution that comes to mind is to just use t-tests (or Chi-2). However, I am unsure if lavaan or SemTool has a function for this already.
>
> # Run Models
>  model1 <- sem(model1, data = data1)
> model2 <- sem(model2, data = data2)
>
>  # Extract the SEs of the parameter estimates
>  summary1 <- summary(model1)
> summary2 <- summary(model2)
>
>  # Extract the path coefficient estimates and SEs
> coef1 <- summary1$coefficients[["IV -> DV"]]
> se1 <- summary1$se[["IV -> DV"]]
> coef2 <- summary2$coefficients[["IV -> DV"]]
>  se2 <- summary2$se[["IV -> DV"]]
>
> Then run a t-test between these values. Ideally, it would be nice to identify the difference between regression parameters required to reach significance. E.g., a difference of .15 is < .01. However, this might not be possible given the differences in error between models.
>
> Kind Regards,
>    Conal

messages.body_plain:
Hi Everyone,

I'm having an issue with constraints behaving weirdly across different ways of specifying the same model. I'm working with the STARTS model, which decomposes variance in multiple waves of a variable (X) into purely stable trait variance, variance that has an autoregressive structure, and state variance unique to each wave.

There are multiple ways to specify this model. For instance, if you predict each observed X from a latent stable trait and a latent autoregressive trait, then the residual can be considered the "state" component of the STARTS model. This should be equivalent to a model that defines an explicit "state" latent variable for each wave, but sets the residual variance of each observed X to 0.

For some extensions that I want to do, I'd prefer to use the latter approach, where I define an explicit latent state variable. However the STARTS usually has a stationarity constraint, and imposing this constraint works when I specify the model the first way, but does not work when I specify it the second way (even though the constraint doesn't refer to this state component or the residuals for the observed variables; it relates to the autoregressive part, which is the same in both).

If I add a stationarity constraint to the first model (shown in the model labeled "starts_c" below), the model runs and the estimates make sense. Hello dear all
I'm running CFA and SEM but I encountered some message errors.
Any help from your side would be greatly appreciated. I'm using matrix correlation. My covariance matrix is not positive definite and I convert it to positive Covariance matrix definite.
When I run the CFA script I get the following error message:
fit.cfaMod<-cfa(cfaMod,sample.cov=Mal5,sample.nobs=1193, estimator = "ML",std.lv <http://std.lv/>=TRUE)
Error in diag(sample.cov[[g]]) : invalid 'nrow' value (too large or NA)
In addition: Warning message:
In diag(sample.cov[[g]]) : NAs introduced by coercion

This my code( The data is attached):

rm(list = ls())
library(GPArotation)
library(psych)
library(ggplot2)
library(lavaan)
library(lavaanPlot)
library(semPlot)
library(semTools)
setwd("~/My topic/My topic/DATA/VALID DATA/Data_final")
Mal<-read.csv("CC_MalariaS.csv",header = TRUE,sep = ",")
str('Mal')
head(Mal)
names(Mal)
attach(Mal)
summary(is.na <http://is.na/>(Mal))
str(Mal)
#### Convert to numerical#############
Mal$Min_Relative.Humidity<-as.numeric(as.factor(Mal$Min_Relative.Humidity))
Mal$Max_Relative.Humidity<-as.numeric(as.factor(Mal$Max_Relative.Humidity))#######
str(Mal)

####Smooth the data(non positive matrix)###########
d<-cor.smooth(Mal)### Smooth the matrix(non positive)
Mal1<-as.data.frame(d)
#a<-is.na <http://is.na/>(Mal1)
#summary(a)
Mal2<-solve(Mal1, tol = 1.47364e-11)
## Scale all the variables ####################
Mal3<-apply(Mal2, 2, scale)

####Covert Non positive cov matrix to positive cov matrix#####
U<-svd(Mal3)$u
D<-svd(Mal3)$d
V<-svd(Mal3)$v

###Transform diagonal value  to positive####
D[D<0]<-0

###Definite the positive matrix######
Mal4<-U%*%diag(D)%*%t(V)

###Name le col and row of Mal4###
colnames(Mal4)=c('Mean_Temperature','Min_Temperature','Max_Temperature',
                  'Mean_Relative.Humidity','Min_Relative.Humidity',
                  'Max_Relative.Humidity','Wind.Speed','Rainfall','Malaria_Incidence')

row.names(Mal4)=c('Mean_Temperature','Min_Temperature','Max_Temperature',
                 'Mean_Relative.Humidity','Min_Relative.Humidity',
                 'Max_Relative.Humidity','Wind.Speed','Rainfall','Malaria_Incidence')
colnames(Mal4)
rownames(Mal4)
Mal5<-table(apply(Mal4,1, paste,collapse=""))
Mal5<-as.data.frame("Mal5")
######simple structure###
threefactor<-fa(data.frame(subsetMal1),nfactors =4,rotate ="oblimin",fm="ML",SMC = T,covar = T)
summary(threefactor)
print(threefactor,cut = 0.3,digits = 2)
fa.diagram(threefactor,sort=TRUE, cut=.3, simple=TRUE, errors=FALSE, digits=2, e.size=.05, rsize=0.15)
plot(threefactor)
g<-fa.plot(threefactor, labels=TRUE)

cfaMod<-'F4=~Rainfall+Min_Relative.Humidity
F1=~Max_Temperature+Mean_Relative.Humidity
F2=~Min_Temperature+Mean_Temperature+Max_Temperature
F3=~Wind.Speed
Malaria_Incidence~F1+F2+F3+F4
Rainfall~~Max_Temperature+Mean_Temperature+Min_Relative.Humidity
+Min_Relative.Humidity+Mean_Relative.Humidity
Mean_Temperature~~Mean_Relative.Humidity+Max_Temperature
+Min_Relative.Humidity+Max_Relative.Humidity
Max_Temperature~~Min_Relative.Humidity+Max_Relative.Humidity+
Malaria_Incidence+Mean_Relative.Humidity
Mean_Relative.Humidity~~Malaria_Incidence
Min_Relative.Humidity~~Max_Relative.Humidity
Wind.Speed~~Malaria_Incidence
F1~~F4'
#### Confimratory Factor Analysis##########
fit.cfaMod<-cfa(cfaMod,sample.cov=Mal5,sample.nobs=1193, estimator = "ML",std.lv <http://std.lv/>=TRUE)
summary(fit.cfaMod,fit.measures=TRUE,standardized=TRUE,rsq=TRUE)

Hello,

I some questions about the model below:

model1 <-
  'A =~ C5_1_C5 + C5_2_C5 + C5_3_C5 + C5_4_C5
   B =~ B5_1_B5 + B5_9_B5 + B5_6_B5 + B5_3_B5

   D =~ E7_6_E7 + E7_10_E7 + E9_1_E9 + E9_4_E9 + E9_5_E9
   E =~ E8_2_E8 + E8_3_E8 + E8_4_E8
   F =~ E6_3_E6 + E6_7_E6 + E6_9_E6
   outcome ~ A + B + C + D + E + F
 E14_3_E14 ~~ E14_4_E14
   E7_6_E7 ~~ E7_10_E7'

model1.fit <- cfa(model = model1,
                  data = data_an,
                  ordered = "outcome",
                  link = "probit")

1. The outcome is binary and coded as 1 or 2. I'm assuming this is fine and that it doesn't need to be 0/1
2. I have declared the outcome to be ordered, but not the variables which make up the factors (which are responses to a likert scale). The lavaan documentation suggests this is acceptable, but I would like to confirm
3. The interpretation of the probit coefficients: is the below acceptable?

The unstandardised effect can be interpreted to mean that when this variable increases by one unit, the z-score for probability of being fully vaccinated decreases by 0.29 units. The standardised coefficient can be interpreted to mean that when this variable is increased by one standard deviation, the z-score score for probability of being fully vaccinated decreases by 0.20 standard deviations.

Thank you,

James

> Hi Everyone,
>
> I'm having an issue with constraints behaving weirdly across different ways of specifying the same model. I'm working with the STARTS model, which decomposes variance in multiple waves of a variable (X) into purely stable trait variance, variance that has an autoregressive structure, and state variance unique to each wave.
>
> There are multiple ways to specify this model. For instance, if you predict each observed X from a latent stable trait and a latent autoregressive trait, then the residual can be considered the "state" component of the STARTS model. This should be equivalent to a model that defines an explicit "state" latent variable for each wave, but sets the residual variance of each observed X to 0.
>
> For some extensions that I want to do, I'd prefer to use the latter approach, where I define an explicit latent state variable. However the STARTS usually has a stationarity constraint, and imposing this constraint works when I specify the model the first way, but does not work when I specify it the second way (even though the constraint doesn't refer to this state component or the residuals for the observed variables; it relates to the autoregressive part, which is the same in both).

In principle, you can bootstrap all conceivable coefficients. The procedure is basically as follows:

(1) Write a function that extracts the desired coefficients. Execute bootstrapLavaan.
(2) Write a function that computes the CI. Pass the object created with bootstrapLavaan.
(3) Print the results.

Here's an example:

library(lavaan)

pop.model <- "
ER =~ 1.0 * socb13 + 1.0 * socb14 + 1.0* socb15 + 1.0 * socb16
WDR =~ 1.0 * socb24 + 1.0 * socb25 + 1.0 * socb26
DAD =~ 1.0 * fatherinvo01 + 1.0 * fatherinvo02 + 1.0 * fatherinvo03 + 1.0 * fatherinvo04 + 1.0 * fatherinvo05
MOM =~ 1.0 * motherinvo01 + 1.0 * motherinvo02 + 1.0 * motherinvo03 + 1.0 * motherinvo04 + 1.0 * motherinvo05

ER ~ 0.3 * DAD + 0.4 * MOM
WDR ~ 0.5 * ER + 0.2 * DAD+ 0.4 * MOM
"

dta <- simulateData(pop.model, sample.nobs = 2000)

model<-
'ER=~socb13+socb14+socb15+socb16
WDR=~socb24+socb25+socb26
DAD=~fatherinvo01+fatherinvo02+fatherinvo03+fatherinvo04+fatherinvo05
MOM=~motherinvo01+motherinvo02+motherinvo03+motherinvo04+motherinvo05

ER~a*DAD+b*MOM
WDR~c*ER+d*DAD+e*MOM

med1 := a*c
med2 := b*c
tot_X1Y := a*c+d
tot_X2Y := b*c+e'

result <- sem(model, dta)

# Std. estimates
get.std <- function(obj) {
  sl <- standardizedsolution(obj)
  res <- sl[, "est.std"]
  names(res) <- paste0(sl[, "lhs"], sl[, "op"], sl[, "rhs"])
  res
}

# 95% perc CI
get.ci <http://get.ci> <- function(obj) {
  alpha <- c(0.025, 0.975)
  ci <- sapply(colnames(obj), function(column, obj, alpha) {
    c(
      ci.lower = as.numeric(quantile(obj[, column], alpha[1], type = 6)),
      ci.upper = as.numeric(quantile(obj[, column], alpha[2], type = 6))
    )
  }, obj, alpha)
  t(ci)
}

boot <- bootstrapLavaan(result, R = 100, FUN = get.std, verbose = TRUE)
ci   <- get.ci <http://get.ci>(boot)

cbind(
  standardizedsolution(result)[, c("lhs", "op", "rhs", "est.std")],
  ci
)

An easy-to-use and more general solution can be found here: https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/0RSsh4M6zQg/m/03uaQYpyAQAJ

Best

Christian

messages.subject: Correlated exogenous variables
messages.subject_clean: Correlated exogenous variables
messages.body_plain:
I have a theoretical question about correlated exogenous variables.
I have a model with two exogenous variables and three endogenous, both
exogenous are regressed against all endogenous. The exogenous variables are
very correlated (>0,7) but I cannot choose between one of them as they
represent different facets of what I’m trying to represent. Therefore I wanted
to include this information in the model, that the variables are correlated. But
I realized that including the covariances ~~ among them didn’t change any of
the coefficients so I believe that the model is not dealing with that
correlation.

How should I approach the correlation of these exogenous
variables? Are there specific guidelines or rationale that I should consider?

messages.subject: Re: Correlated exogenous variables
messages.subject_clean: Correlated exogenous variables
messages.body_plain:
This may be a lavaan question. Perhaps the covariance is already in your model, though not displayed because by default the exogenous variables are treated as fixed (fixed.x = TRUE) and so the covariance is not a free parameter? This is an example:

library(lavaan)
#> This is lavaan 0.6-13
#> lavaan is FREE software! Please report any bugs.
set.seed(68942)
n <- 100
x <- MASS::mvrnorm(n,
                   mu = c(x1 = 0, x2 = 0),
                   Sigma = matrix(c(1, .7, .7, 1), 2, 2))
y <- .3 * x[, 1] + .4 * x[, 2] + rnorm(n, 0, .8)
dat <- data.frame(x, y)
model <-
"
y ~ x1 + x2
"
fit <- sem(model, data = dat)
summary(fit)
#> lavaan 0.6.13 ended normally after 1 iteration
#>
#>   Estimator                                         ML
#>   Optimization method                           NLMINB
#>   Number of model parameters                         3
#>
#>   Number of observations                           100
#>
#> Model Test User Model:
#>
#>   Test statistic                                 0.000
#>   Degrees of freedom                                 0
#>
#> Parameter Estimates:
#>
#>   Standard errors                             Standard
#>   Information                                 Expected
#>   Information saturated (h1) model          Structured
#>
#> Regressions:
#>                    Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)
#>   y ~
#>     x1                0.171    0.104    1.645    0.100
#>     x2                0.360    0.110    3.278    0.001
#>
#> Variances:
#>                    Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)
#>    .y                 0.623    0.088    7.071    0.000

parameterEstimates(fit)
#>   lhs op rhs   est    se     z pvalue ci.lower ci.upper
#> 1   y  ~  x1 0.171 0.104 1.645  0.100   -0.033    0.375
#> 2   y  ~  x2 0.360 0.110 3.278  0.001    0.145    0.575
#> 3   y ~~   y 0.623 0.088 7.071  0.000    0.450    0.795
#> 4  x1 ~~  x1 1.025 0.000    NA     NA    1.025    1.025
#> 5  x1 ~~  x2 0.642 0.000    NA     NA    0.642    0.642
#> 6  x2 ~~  x2 0.919 0.000    NA     NA    0.919    0.919

The covariance, x1 ~~ x2, is in the model but is fixed to its sample value (so are the variances of x1 and x2). It is not displayed by summary() but can be found in the output of parameterEstimates().

If you manually add the covariance, e.g., x1 ~~ x2 in the example above, fixed.x will be set to FALSE. The covariance will then be displayed because it is a free parameter:

model2 <-
"
y ~ x1 + x2
x1 ~~ x2
"
fit2 <- sem(model2, data = dat)
summary(fit2)
#> lavaan 0.6.13 ended normally after 15 iterations
#>
#>   Estimator                                         ML
#>   Optimization method                           NLMINB
#>   Number of model parameters                         6
#>
#>   Number of observations                           100
#>
#> Model Test User Model:
#>
#>   Test statistic                                 0.000
#>   Degrees of freedom                                 0
#>
#> Parameter Estimates:
#>
#>   Standard errors                             Standard
#>   Information                                 Expected
#>   Information saturated (h1) model          Structured
#>
#> Regressions:
#>                    Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)
#>   y ~
#>     x1                0.171    0.104    1.645    0.100
#>     x2                0.360    0.110    3.278    0.001
#>
#> Covariances:
#>                    Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)
#>   x1 ~~
#>     x2                0.642    0.116    5.516    0.000
#>
#> Variances:
#>                    Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)
#>    .y                 0.623    0.088    7.071    0.000
#>     x1                1.025    0.145    7.071    0.000
#>     x2                0.919    0.130    7.071    0.000

parameterEstimates(fit2)
#>   lhs op rhs   est    se     z pvalue ci.lower ci.upper
#> 1   y  ~  x1 0.171 0.104 1.645  0.100   -0.033    0.375
#> 2   y  ~  x2 0.360 0.110 3.278  0.001    0.145    0.575
#> 3  x1 ~~  x2 0.642 0.116 5.516  0.000    0.414    0.870
#> 4   y ~~   y 0.623 0.088 7.071  0.000    0.450    0.795
#> 5  x1 ~~  x1 1.025 0.145 7.071  0.000    0.741    1.309
#> 6  x2 ~~  x2 0.919 0.130 7.071  0.000    0.665    1.174

Maybe that is why the results are similar for other parameters in your model?

-- Shu Fai

> This may be a lavaan question. Perhaps the covariance is already in your model, though not displayed because by default the exogenous variables are treated as fixed (fixed.x = TRUE) and so the covariance is not a free parameter? This is an example:
>
> library(lavaan)
> #> This is lavaan 0.6-13
> #> lavaan is FREE software! Please report any bugs.
> set.seed(68942)
> n <- 100
> x <- MASS::mvrnorm(n,
>                    mu = c(x1 = 0, x2 = 0),
>                    Sigma = matrix(c(1, .7, .7, 1), 2, 2))
> y <- .3 * x[, 1] + .4 * x[, 2] + rnorm(n, 0, .8)
> dat <- data.frame(x, y)
> model <-
> "
> y ~ x1 + x2
> "
> fit <- sem(model, data = dat)
> summary(fit)
> #> lavaan 0.6.13 ended normally after 1 iteration

A constant shift only impacts the mean, not the factor loading. Think of
correlation: the correlation between a and b is the same as the
correlation between (a+10) and b.

messages.subject: Re: Understanding USRMR and SRMR output under DWLS
messages.subject_clean: Understanding USRMR and SRMR output under DWLS
messages.body_plain:
> Why does Lavaan report correlations, thresholds, and totals under DWLS
> but only covariance under ML?

It looks likes the DWLS run was treating the variables as categorical.
Then you get (tetrachoric/polychoric) correlations and thresholds.

In the ML run, you treated (implicitly?) the variables as continuous.
And therefore, there is only a covariance matrix. If you add
meanstructure = TRUE, there will also be a mean component.

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
You are seeing the effect of std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE, which fixes the latent
variances to unity in the *first* group (only) when group.equal =
"loadings", but allows them to be free in the remaining groups.

As a result, switching the groups results in a different scale that is
used. Note that the standardized solutions are identical:

lavInspect(fit1, "std")$`1`$lambda
lavInspect(fit2, "std")$`1`$lambda

Yves.

messages.subject: Re: Latent Interactions and "covariance matrix of latent variables is not positive definite"
messages.subject_clean: Latent Interactions and "covariance matrix of latent variables is not positive definite"
messages.body_plain:
They are warnings, not error messages.

> Warning messages:
> 1: In lav_data_full(data = data, group = group, cluster = cluster,  :
>    lavaan WARNING: 107 cases were deleted due to missing values in
>            exogenous variable(s), while fixed.x = TRUE.

This one is harmless, and just points out that have 'lost' 107 cases,
because they had missing values on exogenous 'x' covariates (and lavaan
uses fixed.x = TRUE per default).

> 2: In lav_object_post_check(object) :
>    lavaan WARNING: covariance matrix of latent variables
>                  is not positive definite;
>                  use lavInspect(fit, "cov.lv <http://cov.lv>") to investigate.

This is a potential sign of model misfit, but it could also be due to a
relatively small sample size. To see the latent covariance matrix in
correlation matrix, you can use lavInspect(fit, "cor.lv <http://cor.lv>")

Yves.

messages.subject: Re: Correlated exogenous variables
messages.subject_clean: Correlated exogenous variables
messages.body_plain:
On 1/29/23 18:24, Erica Rievrs wrote:
> Thank you a lot for your clear answer! Yes, they are present in the
> model parameters estimates, I had not realized that before.
> Does that mean then that lavaan automatically deals with
> multicollinearity issues in the model?

Not quite. lavaan (by default) treats exogenous (observed) 'x'
covariates as fixed. As a result, you don't need to worry about their
correlation structure. It is just not part of the model.

>   Do you have by any chance any literature on that subject to indicate?

Think of a regression model Y ~ X1 + X2 + X3. Usually, we treat X1/X2/X3
as 'fixed', and we don't care if they are correlated or not. We just
want to estimate the regression coefficients (and the residual
variance). This corresponds to lavaan's fixed.x = TRUE.

Yves.

messages.subject: Re: Latent Interactions and "covariance matrix of latent variables is not positive definite"
messages.subject_clean: Latent Interactions and "covariance matrix of latent variables is not positive definite"
messages.body_plain:
In this case, I think the warning might be a sign of model misspecification. When one of the variables used for the interaction term has a single indicator you don't want to include residual covariances for the interaction latent variable since this ends up being redundant with the latent interaction variables (here you're trying to estimate the latent variable and all residual covariances among the indicators for each latent interaction variable). I'd remove all the residual covariances at the end.

Alex

On Monday, January 30, 2023 at 9:47:20 AM UTC-5 yros...@gmail.com wrote:
> They are warnings, not error messages.
>
> > Warning messages:
> > 1: In lav_data_full(data = data, group = group, cluster = cluster,  :
> >   lavaan WARNING: 107 cases were deleted due to missing values in
> >           exogenous variable(s), while fixed.x = TRUE.
>
> This one is harmless, and just points out that have 'lost' 107 cases,
> because they had missing values on exogenous 'x' covariates (and lavaan
> uses fixed.x = TRUE per default).
>
> > 2: In lav_object_post_check(object) :
> >   lavaan WARNING: covariance matrix of latent variables
> >                 is not positive definite;
> >                 use lavInspect(fit, "cov.lv <http://cov.lv>") to investigate.
>
> This is a potential sign of model misfit, but it could also be due to a
> relatively small sample size. To see the latent covariance matrix in
> correlation matrix, you can use lavInspect(fit, "cor.lv <http://cor.lv>")
>
> Yves.

Thank you,

messages.subject: Re: Running CFA binary variables return low factor loading
messages.subject_clean: Running CFA binary variables return low factor loading
messages.body_plain:
Phuct,
You need to consider whether these are raw or standardized loadings.  It is also relevant whether you are treating the non-binary items as ordinal, or as continuous.   Raw loadings are sensitive to the standard deviations of the items (and latent variables).  In a model with thresholds, this applies to the scaling of the unobserved continuous item variable.

These things can get a little tricky because you want to evaluate the validity of the observed scores, not the unobserved continuous item variables.  You may want to examine the estimated thresholds for the binary items to see if they are extreme.  It may also be helpful to examine some classical item analysis indices like the correlations between the binary items and the corresponding adjusted sum scores (i.e., sum score minus the item score) and the univariate frequency tables for the items.

Sometimes with knowledge tests, the domain of knowledge is very large.  As a result, each item in the sample of items may have a relatively low correlation with knowledge of the overall domain and with other items in the domain.  This is particularly likely if the test is designed to include items with a wide range of item difficulties.  Nonetheless, in a long enough test, positive manifold can still produce a reliable test.  The probability of a person with high knowledge getting most of the items wrong on a very short test may be non-negligibly high but the same probability for a longer test may become very small.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/
